# 2. Data

## 2.1 Data sources and construction

This study uses farm-level data from the three most recent Ghana Living Standards Surveys: GLSS5, conducted in 2005/06; GLSS6, conducted in 2012/13; and GLSS7, conducted in 2016/17. The GLSS surveys are repeated cross-sectional household surveys that use a two-stage sampling design, with enumeration areas selected in the first stage and households selected in the second stage. We rely on the consolidated farmer-level GLSS dataset developed by (Tsiboe 2020), which harmonizes farm production outcomes across survey rounds and has been used to study agricultural productivity across multiple Ghanaian crop value chains (Tsiboe et al. 2019, 2021a, 2021b, 2022; Tsiboe 2021).

Although the consolidated dataset provides harmonized farm-level outcomes, it does not directly contain the community-level agricultural service provision indicators required for this study. To construct these measures, we returned to the original GLSS household and community files, which preserve the enumeration area, household, and member identifiers needed to link farm operators to their community service environment. Agricultural service variables are generated from the agriculture section of the GLSS community questionnaires and merged into the farmer-level dataset using survey and enumeration-area identifiers.

Community agricultural service variables are harmonized using GLSS7 as the reference structure. In GLSS7, the relevant variables are cs5q5--cs5q15, which cover the presence and distance of agricultural extension offices, extension officer presence and visits, extension-service provider agencies, services provided by extension agents, compliance with extension guidance, agricultural or fishing associations, association services, cooperative participation, and tractor availability. Equivalent questions from earlier survey rounds are mapped into the GLSS7 naming and coding structure before the community files are appended. GLSS6 is largely comparable to GLSS7, while GLSS5 requires selected renaming because the association, cooperative, and tractor questions are shifted relative to the GLSS7 structure. After harmonization, the data are collapsed to the survey-community level and merged with household and farm records. Detailed variable definitions and GLSS7 source-question references are provided in Appendix Note S1, Table S1, while the cross-round harmonization procedure is documented in Appendix A, Table S2.

For the meta-stochastic frontier analysis, we use two complementary sets of agricultural service measures. The first captures the institutional source of service delivery, distinguishing communities with any agricultural service source, agricultural or fishing associations, agricultural cooperatives, and active extension delivery. Active extension delivery is defined as farmer-facing extension support, reflected by extension officer visits or stronger combinations of extension access, rather than the passive presence of an extension office alone. The second set captures the content of services available to farmers, including planting or seed-use support, mechanization or agricultural equipment, credit, irrigation, animal husbandry, fertilizer or agrochemical input support, and post-harvest, marketing, or storage support. Together, these measures allow us to evaluate whether farm performance, technical efficiency, and technology gaps vary not only with access to agricultural services, but also with the source and type of support available in the community.

The analysis is restricted to crop farmers with reported yields, measured in kilograms per hectare, between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within each survey round and crop. The final sample includes 22,519 farm operators cultivating at least one of the following crops: banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus fruits, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton, kenaf, maize, millet, oil palm, peanuts, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other reported crops.
